title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
statement: Design a data structure that supports two operations. addWord(word) stores a word made of lowercase letters. search(pattern) returns true if any stored word matches the pattern, where the pattern is lowercase letters plus the wildcard character . which matches exactly one letter. A pattern matches only words of the same length: . matches one character, never zero and never several.
realWorld: A dictionary service behind spell-check or a command palette: the word list is loaded once at start-up and then queried millions of times, some of those queries carrying a single-character wildcard (c.t). Per-query cost is the only cost that matters, so the shape of the stored dictionary is the whole design decision.

examples.input: addWord(bad), addWord(dad), addWord(mad), then search(pad), search(bad), search(.ad), search(b..)
examples.explanation: pad was never added. bad is an exact hit. .ad matches bad, dad and mad, so one hit is enough. b.. matches bad: the first character is pinned, the other two are free.

examples.input: addWord(a), addWord(ab), then search(a.), search(.a), search(..)
examples.explanation: a. matches ab. .a is false even though a is stored, because the pattern has length 2 and a has length 1. .. matches ab, showing that length, not content, is what rules a word in or out first.
Three dots match abc. Four dots match nothing: a dot is one character, so the pattern can never stretch to cover a shorter word.

constraints: word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters
word in search consists of lowercase English letters and at most 3 dots
At most 10^4 calls to addWord and search in total

bruteForce.idea: Keep every word in a list. To search, walk the list and compare the pattern against each word of the right length, treating a dot as an automatic match.

complexity.time: O(n * L) per search, for n stored words of length up to L

bruteForce.whySlow: Every search re-reads the entire dictionary, and nearly all of that reading re-makes decisions that were already made. Searching ba. against ten thousand words that start with z compares b against z ten thousand separate times: one first-character decision, repeated once per word, when all those words share that one first character. The words that share a prefix are never allowed to share the work of rejecting it.

patternIdentification: A dictionary that is queried character by character, where many words share leading characters, is a trie: the shared prefix is stored once, so one comparison rules out an entire subtree instead of one word. The wildcard then changes only how you move through it. A fixed character follows exactly one child, so the lookup is a walk down a single path; a dot has no child to pick, so it must follow all of them, and the walk becomes a depth-first search over the trie. Whenever a lookup step has more than one legal continuation, keep the data structure and upgrade the traversal to a search.

optimized.idea: Store the words in a 26-way trie. Search is a recursion over (position in the pattern, node in the trie). A letter descends into the single matching child and fails immediately if it is absent. A dot recurses into every non-null child and succeeds if any of them does. The pattern is matched only when the recursion reaches its end on a node marked as a word, which is what keeps a stored prefix like ba from matching when only bad was added. Be honest about the cost: with d dots the branching is up to 26^d, and a pattern of nothing but dots visits every node of the trie, so its cost is the size of the whole dictionary. The constraint capping dots at 3 is what keeps that acceptable.

complexity.time: addWord O(L). search O(L) with no dots; up to O(26^d * L) with d dots, and an all-dots pattern touches every trie node, which is O(N) for N characters stored
complexity.space: O(N) for the trie plus O(L) recursion depth

if (node == null) return false;                  // the letter had no child: dead end

if (c != '.') return dfs(pattern, at + 1, node.children[c - 'a']);   // one fixed child
for (Node child : node.children)                 // a dot: branch into all of them

commonMistakes: Returning true as soon as the pattern is consumed instead of returning node.isWord - after adding only bad, search(ba) reports true, because the path ba exists in the trie even though no word ends there.

In the dot branch, returning the result of the first non-null child rather than continuing the loop - with bad and cat stored, search(.at) descends into b first, fails there and returns false, silently skipping the c subtree that does match.

Indexing node.children[c - 'a'] and recursing without the null guard at the top of dfs - the first search for a letter never added, such as search(zzz) on an all-lowercase-a dictionary, throws NullPointerException instead of returning false.
